title: Auroras: the Sun's wind on Earth's magnet
interaction: Earth with its magnetic field drawn as loops, in a stream of charged specks from the Sun; press play and the specks cannot cross the field lines, so they slide along them and spiral down into the air in two rings around the magnetic poles, where the sky glows green and, higher up, red. The one control is the strength of the solar wind. A gust squeezes the field and the glowing rings widen toward the equator, which is when people far from the poles get to see the lights.
takeaway: Auroras happen in rings around the magnetic poles because Earth's magnetic field steers the Sun's charged particles there, and a stronger solar wind pushes the rings toward the equator.
needsSource: none (charged particles integrated in a dipole field, the field's sunward edge pushed in by solar-wind pressure, glow colour by height; the page states the simplification that particles are shown guided straight down the field lines, where the real ones arrive by way of the night-side tail; the NOAA SWPC OVATION aurora forecast, public domain, can be shown for comparison)
pitfall: Auroras are not sunlight reflected off polar ice, and they are not in the clouds: they glow a hundred kilometres up and higher.
why: NASA Space Place, 'What Is an Aurora?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/aurora/en/).
overlapWith: electromagnetism (level 2) shows charges moving in fields in the abstract; this page shows it once, on a planet, with the pattern it makes in the sky.

title: Comets and their tails
interaction: Scrub a comet along its real stretched orbit, far out and frozen, then swinging in close to the Sun. As it warms, gas and dust stream off it, and the tail always points away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is going, so on the way out the comet flies tail-first. Two tails appear: a straight blue gas tail pushed by the solar wind and a curved dust tail of grains that lag along the orbit; zoom in to see the grains leave.
takeaway: A comet's tail is blown by the Sun, not left behind by motion, so it always points away from the Sun and the comet travels tail-first when it leaves.
needs: Orbital elements of one or two real comets (Halley, and a recent bright one) from the JPL Small-Body Database API (https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/sbdb.html); NASA/JPL data with no separate licence text, free to use with the credit 'Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech' under JPL's use policy. Treat as open but confirm against the API's terms before shipping.
needsSource: JPL Small-Body Database orbital elements (NASA/JPL, free with credit; no explicit data licence)
pitfall: The tail does not trail behind like exhaust, and a comet is not a burning rock: it is ice and dust turning to gas in sunlight.
why: NASA Space Place, 'What Is a Comet?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/comets/en/); England KS2 Year 5, the movement of bodies relative to the Sun.
overlapWith: orbits-kepler (level 1) launches bodies into ellipses; this page uses one real ellipse and asks only which way the tail points.

title: Why the sky is dark at night
interaction: Stand in a forest drawn from above and widen it: with a few trees you see out between the trunks, but keep adding trees farther away and every line of sight ends on bark, so the forest closes into a wall. Then swap trees for stars scattered through space at their real sparseness and press play: light from the stars has been travelling only as long as the universe has existed, so only the stars within that distance can be seen, and a counter shows the sky is still almost entirely black. Drag the age of the universe up and watch the sky slowly fill; it would take an unimaginably longer time than the real one before the night sky glowed like the Sun's surface everywhere.
takeaway: In an endless forest of stars shining forever, every direction would end on a star and the night sky would blaze; it is dark because the universe has an age, so the light from most of those stars has not arrived yet.
needsSource: none (the fraction of the sky covered by stars of a given size scattered at a given density out to the light-travel distance, computed by counting lines of sight; the page states the simplification that it ignores the stretching of light by the expansion of space, which darkens the sky further)
pitfall: The sky is not dark because stars are too far or too faint, or because dust hides them: with endless stars for endless time the faint ones would add up and the dust would glow too. It is dark because light has had only a limited time to travel.
why: Olbers' paradox is a standing popular question: Scientific American, 'Why Is the Sky Dark at Night? You Can Thank the Big Bang' (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-is-the-night-sky-dark-olbers); the MinutePhysics video 'Why is it dark at night?' (https://www.universetoday.com/97678/video-why-is-the-sky-dark-at-night).
overlapWith: big-bang (level 2) runs the expansion and the timeline of the universe; this page uses only one consequence of the universe having an age, that light has had limited time to travel, and never mentions expansion on the stage.

title: Earth is a ball
interaction: Drag a ship out to sea and watch it from the shore: on a flat world it only shrinks, but on the round one its hull disappears before its sails as the sea bulges up between you and it, and climbing a cliff brings it back into view. Then walk a little figure around the globe: wherever it stands its feet point to the middle, and a dropped ball falls toward the middle too, so nobody on the far side falls off.
takeaway: The world is a ball, so the sea itself hides the bottom of a distant ship, and 'down' means toward the middle wherever you stand.
needsSource: none (the geometry of a sphere: horizon distance from eye height and the height hidden beyond it; gravity drawn toward the centre)
pitfall: People on the far side are not upside down and do not have to hold on: the page draws no up arrow anywhere. And the ship does not vanish because it got too small.
why: NGSS 5-PS2-1: 'Support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down', with 'down' pointing toward the center of the spherical Earth (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/5-ps2-1-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions); England KS2 Year 5: 'describe the sun, Earth and moon as approximately spherical bodies'.
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon (level 1) tilts and orbits the Earth; this page never moves it, only shows that it is round and which way down is.

title: Leap years: why February gets an extra day
interaction: A calendar wheel turns inside Earth's orbit: one lap of the Sun takes 365 days and about a quarter more, so each New Year falls a quarter-day short. Scrub forward with no leap days and watch the first day of summer slide through the calendar, a month after a century and into winter after seven or eight centuries; switch on 'one extra day every four years' and the slide almost stops; zoom out over a thousand years to see the small drift that is left and the 'skip every hundred, keep every four hundred' rule that fixes it.
takeaway: A year is not a whole number of days, so a calendar without leap days drifts out of step with the seasons; an extra day every four years, with a few skipped, keeps them matched.
pitfall: A leap day fixes the calendar, not the orbit; nothing about the seasons changes. The rule is not simply every four years: 1900 was not a leap year and 2000 was.
why: NASA/JPL Education, 'Doing the math on why we have leap day' (interest spikes every leap year): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/doing-the-math-on-why-we-have-leap-day/
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon: why there are seasons; this page is why the calendar needs correcting to stay lined up with them.
needsSource: none

title: Rockets: going up by throwing things down
interaction: Stand on a skateboard and throw a ball: you roll the other way, and the harder or heavier the throw the faster you roll; throw a bag of balls one after another and you keep speeding up. Then pump up a bottle rocket on the lawn: water is thrown out of the neck and the bottle shoots up, and sliding the water fill from empty to full finds the amount that goes highest. Launch the same rocket in a vacuum chamber and on the Moon and it still goes.
takeaway: A rocket climbs by throwing something out of its back as fast as it can, and it needs nothing to push against, so it works just as well in empty space.
pitfall: A rocket does not push against the air or the ground: it pushes against what it throws out, which is why it works in a vacuum. A full bottle is not best: too much water leaves no room for the air that pushes it out, and too little gives nothing to throw.
why: NASA, 'Activity four: optimize a water rocket engine' (grades 5 to 8, aligned to MS-PS2-2), https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/sls-activity-four-optimize-a-water-rocket.pdf
overlapWith: rockets: that page is the velocity budget, staging and transfer orbits at level 2; this page is only the throwing itself, on a skateboard and in a bottle, and which water fill lifts a bottle highest.
needsSource: none

title: Satellites: the ones that race and the one that stays
interaction: Scrub a day and watch the Space Station lap the Earth sixteen times in a band of tracks that shifts each lap as the Earth turns beneath it, while a TV satellite far higher hangs over one spot and a weather satellite in between keeps its own count. Stand in your town and the sky view shows when the Station crosses overhead and why it is seen only just after dusk or before dawn: it must be in sunlight while you are in shadow. Drag a satellite higher and watch it slow and take longer round.
takeaway: Low satellites race round the Earth many times a day while one special height keeps pace with the turning ground, and a satellite is seen only when the Sun lights it while you are in the dark.
needs: The Space Station's orbital elements from NASA (public domain, e.g. the ISS trajectory data behind Spot the Station) and the altitudes of a named weather and TV satellite from their operators' public pages. CelesTrak two-line elements would be convenient but their redistribution terms are not clearly open, so the page must not depend on them.
pitfall: Satellites do not stay up because there is no gravity in space: the Station is falling all the time and only misses the ground because it is moving sideways so fast. A satellite that seems to hang still is not stopped; it is racing round once a day, exactly as fast as the ground beneath it turns.
why: NASA Spot the Station, a service built around the public's question of when the Station can be seen, https://spotthestation.nasa.gov/ (curriculum: NGSS MS-ESS1-2, gravity and orbits)
overlapWith: orbits-kepler: that page launches a body and derives Kepler's laws; this page launches nothing, it scrubs real satellites by height and the geometry of seeing them. gps, at level 2, is what one constellation is for.
needsSource: NASA ISS trajectory data (public domain, https://spotthestation.nasa.gov/); operator pages for a GOES-class weather satellite and a geostationary TV satellite.

title: Shooting stars: what burns up and what gets through
interaction: Drop a space pebble into the top of the air at twenty kilometres a second and watch: it rams the air so hard that the air in front glows and the pebble boils away, a streak a hundred kilometres up that lasts a second. The one control is the size of the rock: a sand grain vanishes in a flash, a fist-sized rock makes a fireball that lasts longer and reaches lower, and a boulder keeps a cold middle all the way down and lands as a meteorite, with a bar showing how much of it is left. A second control changes the speed.
takeaway: A shooting star is a grain of dust heating the air by hitting it so fast that the air glows, a hundred kilometres up; only a rock big enough to keep a cold middle reaches the ground.
needsSource: none (the single-body meteoroid equations: drag, mass loss and glow through the US Standard Atmosphere 1976, public domain, the same atmosphere the rockets and flight pages already use)
pitfall: A meteor is not heated by friction rubbing on the air but by the air it squeezes in front of it, and a meteorite is not hot when it lands. A shooting star is not a star.
why: NASA Space Place, 'Asteroid or Meteor: What's the Difference?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/asteroid-or-meteor/en/) and 'What Is a Meteor Shower?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/meteor-shower/en/).
overlapWith: rockets (level 2) flies up through the same atmosphere model; this page falls through it, and no existing page shows anything burning up on entry.

title: The solar system to scale
interaction: Start with Earth as a marble and zoom out along a line drawn to one true scale, sizes and distances alike: the Moon is a pea thirty marbles away, the Sun is a ball as tall as a child a hundred and fifty metres down the street, and the outer planets are specks far beyond. Press play to send a flash of light from the Sun and watch the clock: it passes Mercury after three minutes, reaches Earth after eight, Jupiter after forty-three, and Neptune after four hours. Zoom all the way out and the planets vanish into the emptiness.
takeaway: The solar system is almost entirely empty space: with Earth a marble, the Sun is a ball as tall as a child far down the street, and even light takes hours to cross the planets.
needs: Planet and Moon diameters, mean distances from the Sun and orbital periods from the NASA NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/), US Government work, public domain.
needsSource: NASA NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet (public domain)
pitfall: No drawing that fits the planets on one page can show both their sizes and their distances; this page never breaks scale, so at most zooms the planets are too small to see, and it says so.
why: NGSS MS-ESS1-3: 'Analyze and interpret data to determine scale properties of objects in the solar system' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess1-3-earths-place-universe); NASA Space Place, 'What Is a Light-Year?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/light-year/en/).
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon (level 1) moves three bodies on a diagram that is not to scale; this page is only scale and light time, with nothing orbiting.

title: The Sun is a star
interaction: The Sun hangs in a black sky; drag it away. As it recedes it shrinks and dims by the same rule as a torch across a field (twice as far, a quarter as bright), until at the distance of the nearest star it is one faint dot among the others. Then the other way: pick a star from the night sky (Sirius, Betelgeuse, Proxima) and drag it in to the Sun's distance, where it is a glaring disc bigger or smaller than ours.
takeaway: The Sun looks nothing like the stars only because it is close: dragged far enough it becomes one of them, and some of them, brought close, would outshine it.
needs: Distances, brightness and colour for a few dozen named stars from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th edition (BSC5), as hosted by NASA HEASARC (https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/W3Browse/star-catalog/bsc5p.html), whose documentation states it is in the public domain; the HYG database v4.2 (https://astronexus.com/hyg, CC BY-SA 4.0) is a share-alike alternative and is not needed.
needsSource: Yale Bright Star Catalogue BSC5 via NASA HEASARC (public domain)
pitfall: The Sun is not a huge or unusual star, and the stars are not small lights: each is a sun. Brightness falls with the square of distance, not in step with it.
why: NGSS 5-ESS1-1: 'Support an argument that the apparent brightness of the sun and stars is due to their relative distances from the Earth' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/5-ess1-1-earths-place-universe); NASA Space Place, 'How Does Our Sun Compare With Other Stars?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/sun-compare/en/).
overlapWith: stars (level 2) runs a star's life on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram; this page never changes a star, only its distance.

title: Day, night and time zones
interaction: A globe lit from one side. Spin it and watch cities pass from night into dawn, noon, dusk and night again; each city has a clock, and the clocks disagree: when it is noon in London it is already evening in Tokyo and still early morning in New York. Drag the hour and the day-night line sweeps round the world once per turn; cross the date line and the calendar flips.
takeaway: There is no single 'now' on the clock: the Sun is overhead at different places at different moments, so clocks are set by how far east or west you live, in strips that go round with the spinning Earth.
needs: Zone offsets from the IANA tz database (https://www.iana.org/time-zones, public domain) and city positions from Natural Earth populated places (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/downloads/10m-cultural-vectors/, public domain). Zone boundaries, if drawn, from timezone-boundary-builder (https://github.com/evansiroky/timezone-boundary-builder, ODbL, share-alike, since Natural Earth's own time-zone layer is believed withdrawn and could not be confirmed); the documented fallback is to draw no boundaries and colour each city by its offset.
needsSource: IANA tz database and Natural Earth populated places (public domain); zone boundaries optional, timezone-boundary-builder (ODbL)
pitfall: The Sun does not go round the Earth, and night is not the Sun switching off: it is the Earth's own shadowed side.
why: England KS2 science, Year 5 Earth and space: 'use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon (level 1) gives day length by latitude and season; this page keeps the tilt out and adds clocks, zones and the date line, which that page does not have.

title: Why stars twinkle (and planets don't)
interaction: Starlight drawn as a thin beam crossing layers of air that drift and wobble, each bending the beam a little, while at the bottom an eye sees the star brighten, fade and jump about. The one control is the star's height above the horizon: low down, the beam crosses far more wobbling air and the twinkling grows wild, and straight overhead it almost stops. Swap the point of light for a small disc, a planet, and the many beams from across the disc average out, so it shines steadily.
takeaway: Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light differently every instant, worst near the horizon, and planets twinkle much less because they are little discs whose many beams average out.
needsSource: none (a stack of drifting random refractive-index layers, ray bending, brightness on a small aperture, the path through air growing as the star nears the horizon)
pitfall: Stars do not flicker themselves, and twinkling says nothing about distance: the same star barely twinkles overhead on a calm night and dances near the horizon.
why: 'Why do stars twinkle' is a standing how-does-it-work question; the Wikipedia article 'Twinkling' explains the turbulence, the horizon effect and why planets twinkle less (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twinkling); England KS3 physics, 'our sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy'.
overlapWith: light-optics (level 1) refracts rays through lenses and prisms with a fixed index; this page has air whose index wobbles in time, which that bench cannot show.

title: What the Moon and the planets are made of
interaction: Pick a world (the Moon, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and the page shows how big it is and how heavy, measured from its pull on the things that orbit it. Fill a ball of its size with layers from a palette of rock, iron, ice and squashed gas until the scale reads right: the Moon fills with rock almost alone, Earth will not get heavy enough without a lump of iron in the middle, Jupiter is nearly all gas squeezed hard, and Saturn comes out lighter than the same ball of water. A last step compares a glass of each world's stuff on a kitchen scale.
takeaway: Weighing a world and measuring its size tells what it is made of without going there: the Moon weighs like rock, Earth is too heavy to be rock alone and must hold iron inside, and Saturn is lighter than water.
needs: Mass, radius and mean density of the Moon and planets from the NASA NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/), US Government work, public domain; densities of rock, iron, ice and water from any standard table.
needsSource: NASA NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet (public domain)
pitfall: Saturn 'floating' is a comparison of density only, not something that could happen; and the Moon is not weightless or hollow: it is a ball of rock whose pull is a sixth of Earth's because it is smaller. The page states that deep inside a giant planet gas is squeezed to the density of water, which is why 'gas' fills Jupiter.
why: NGSS MS-ESS1-3: 'Analyze and interpret data to determine scale properties of objects in the solar system' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess1-3-earths-place-universe); 'would Saturn float on water' is a standing popular question (https://www.worldatlas.com/space/would-saturn-float-on-water.html).
overlapWith: earthquakes (level 1) finds Earth's iron core from seismic waves; this page finds it from weight and size alone, and no existing page says what the Moon or the giant planets are made of.

title: Telescopes
interaction: Trace rays through a refractor and a reflector, drag the eyepiece to focus and read the magnification; then point the telescope at a pair of stars and shrink the aperture until their blurred images, computed from diffraction, merge into one, and widen it to gather more light until a faint star appears. Compare the eye, a 10 cm amateur scope, a 1 m observatory and a 6.5 m space telescope on the same star field, switch on atmospheric seeing to see why the big ground mirror is still blurred, and change the wavelength to see why a radio telescope must be enormous.
takeaway: A telescope's power is in its aperture, not its magnification: a wider mirror gathers more light and resolves finer detail, and the limit set by the wave nature of light is why radio dishes are huge and the sharpest telescopes are in space.
needsSource: none; the Airy pattern and light-gathering are computed, and a synthetic star field needs no catalogue
pitfall: Magnification is cheap and is not the point; a small telescope at high power shows a bigger blur. The blur limit comes from diffraction at the aperture, not from lens flaws, and the atmosphere, not the mirror, limits most ground telescopes.
why: AQA A-level Physics 7408 astrophysics option: refracting and reflecting telescopes, resolving power and the Rayleigh criterion, CCDs https://egglescliffe.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Physics-A-Level-Revision-Checklist-2025-26.pdf
overlapWith: light-optics traces rays through single lenses and mirrors on a bench; this page assembles them into an instrument and adds what ray tracing cannot show, the diffraction limit. The pool's aperture-synthesis (level 3) is interferometry; this is the single-aperture page the earth-sky-weather lens asked another lens to write.

title: Interferometry & aperture synthesis
interaction: Place radio dishes on a map and pick a model sky; every pair of dishes samples one point of the sky's Fourier transform, and as the Earth turns each pair traces an arc in the uv plane. Watch the dirty beam and the dirty image form from whatever the array has sampled: two dishes see only stripes, a dozen over six hours see the source. Run CLEAN step by step, subtracting the beam from the brightest point until the image emerges, and compare it with the truth; shrink the array to lose resolution, spread it to lose the extended emission.
takeaway: An array of small telescopes can see as sharply as one dish as wide as the array, because what it measures is the sky's Fourier transform, and the Earth's rotation fills in the gaps.
pitfall: An interferometer does not gain the collecting area of a filled dish, only its resolution, and the dirty image is not a photograph of the sky but of what was sampled.
why: NRAO Synthesis Imaging Workshop, the graduate course on aperture synthesis theory and technique: https://aas.org/events/2022-02/18th-synthesis-imaging-workshop
overlapWith: light-optics: that page forms images with lenses; this page forms an image with no lens at all, from the correlations between separated telescopes.
needsSource: none

title: What an asteroid does when it hits
interaction: Choose an impactor's size, density, speed and angle and integrate its fall through the atmosphere step by step: drag slows it, heating ablates it, and when the air's ram pressure exceeds its strength it spreads and bursts, its energy released as an airburst at a height the page reports (Chelyabinsk and Tunguska are presets with their published sizes). A body that survives hits the ground: the page scales the crater from the energy and the target rock, then draws rings of effects against distance, the fireball's thermal pulse, the air blast, the ground shaking and the ejecta, over a map at scale. Compare 20 m, 100 m, 1 km and 10 km bodies on one chart.
takeaway: Small asteroids never reach the ground: the air stops them and they burst high up; bodies above about a hundred metres cross the atmosphere as if it were not there, and their effects on the ground scale with their energy in published ways.
needs: The published entry, cratering and effects equations (Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005, and the program's documentation PDF) and literature parameters for Chelyabinsk and Tunguska.
pitfall: A meteor does not burn up by combustion; it is stopped and shattered by air pressure, and an airburst is itself the hazard. The effect scalings are published fits valid over stated ranges, not a dataset; show their limits.
why: The Earth Impact Effects Program (Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005) is the public calculator behind every popular asteroid-impact simulator, and Veritasium's asteroid video is among its most-viewed: https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/ImpactEarth/ImpactEffects
overlapWith: deep-time: the Chicxulub impact as a point on the timeline. shooting-stars (pool, level 0): a sand grain to a boulder entering the air with size as the one control; this page continues to the bodies that survive the air, with fragmentation, airbursts, craters and the published scaling of effects.
needsSource: Published equations in Meteoritics & Planetary Science 40, 817-840 (2005) and the Imperial documentation; not a dataset. Chelyabinsk parameters from Popova et al. 2013 (cited).

title: Planetary atmospheres & escape
interaction: Pick a body (Earth, Mars, Venus, Titan, the Moon, a hot Jupiter) or set mass, radius and exobase temperature, and pick a gas. The page draws the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution against the escape speed and integrates the tail into the Jeans escape flux, then converts it into the time to lose the atmosphere. A chart of escape speed against temperature places every solar-system body and every gas on either side of the diagonal that separates kept from lost; push the Jeans parameter below about three and the escape turns hydrodynamic, with the whole atmosphere blowing off as a wind.
takeaway: Whether a world keeps a gas depends on the race between its escape speed and the gas's thermal speed, which is why the Moon is bare, Mars lost its water's hydrogen, and Earth keeps nitrogen but leaks hydrogen.
needs: Planetary masses, radii and exobase temperatures (NASA planetary fact sheets, US government work; retyped numbers).
pitfall: Thermal escape is molecule by molecule from the tail of the distribution, so a gas is never lost all at once; and Mars lost its air mainly because it is small, not only because it lost its magnetic field.
why: University of Arizona PTYS 595B Escape of Planetary Atmospheres (Jeans, hydrodynamic and nonthermal escape): https://lpl.arizona.edu/node/3594
overlapWith: exoplanets: that page places a planet in the habitable zone by its orbit; this page asks whether it can hold an atmosphere at all, which the zone alone does not decide.
needsSource: NASA planetary fact-sheet values (US government work; retyped numbers).

title: The CMB power spectrum
interaction: Each wavelength of the early universe's photon-baryon fluid is a driven, damped oscillator in the tight-coupling approximation; the page integrates a few hundred of them through recombination and projects the result onto the sky to draw the angular power spectrum, with the Planck 2018 measurements as points. Slide the baryon density and the odd peaks rise against the even ones; slide the dark-matter density and the peaks shift and shrink; curve the universe and every peak slides in angle. The sound horizon and the angular-diameter distance are drawn as the two rulers behind the first peak.
takeaway: The peaks in the CMB are the sound waves of the first 380,000 years frozen on the sky, and their positions and relative heights read off the universe's contents and geometry.
needs: The Planck 2018 TT binned power spectrum from the ESA Planck Legacy Archive (publicly downloadable; the ESA Space Science Archives terms seen in this round are CC BY-NC 3.0 IGO, so the data are not openly licensed in the task's sense and the candidate is weaker for it).
pitfall: The peaks are not harmonics of one note and the spectrum is not an ordinary Fourier transform of a sound; and the tight-coupling model is an approximation stated as such, not a replacement for a Boltzmann code.
why: Wayne Hu's CMB tutorial on the acoustic peaks and baryon loading, the standard teaching reference: https://background.uchicago.edu/~whu/intermediate/intermediate.html
overlapWith: big-bang: that page shows the CMB as a moment on the timeline; this page reads the cosmological parameters off its spectrum.
needsSource: Planck 2018 TT spectrum from the ESA Planck Legacy Archive; the ESA archive terms seen were CC BY-NC 3.0 IGO (non-commercial), so not openly licensed in the task's sense.

title: The cosmic distance ladder
interaction: Climb the ladder one rung at a time. Measure a parallax with the reader's chosen baseline and precision and see how far it reaches; use those distances to calibrate the Cepheid period-luminosity relation from real Cepheids, and the Cepheids in a few nearby galaxies to calibrate the peak brightness of Type Ia supernovae; use the supernovae in the Hubble flow to read the Hubble constant. At each rung the reader sets the measurement error and watches it propagate up the ladder into the error bar on the expansion rate, and the last rung shows the gap between the ladder's value and the CMB's.
takeaway: Every cosmic distance stands on a nearer one, so the uncertainty in the size of the universe is built, rung by rung, from the uncertainty of a parallax.
needs: Gaia DR3 parallaxes for nearby Cepheids (free to use with credit to ESA/Gaia/DPAC; not a Creative Commons licence), OGLE Magellanic Cloud Cepheids for the period-luminosity relation (public download; licence not confirmed), and the Pantheon+/SH0ES distance tables (public download; licence not confirmed).
pitfall: The Hubble tension is a disagreement between two careful measurements, not a mistake in one of them; show both error bars.
why: 3Blue1Brown's two-part video with Terence Tao on the cosmic distance ladder (2025): https://3blue1brown.substack.com/p/the-cosmic-distance-ladder-with-terence
overlapWith: big-bang: that page shows galaxies receding faster with distance; this page is how those distances are measured and how the errors stack up.
needsSource: Gaia DR3 (free with credit, no CC licence); OGLE Cepheids (public download, licence not confirmed); Pantheon+/SH0ES tables (GitHub, licence not confirmed).

title: Cosmic rays & air showers
interaction: Step a cosmic ray into the atmosphere generation by generation in the Heitler-Matthews model: each particle travels one interaction length and splits, neutral pions decay to photons, and the cascade doubles until the particles fall below the critical energy and stop multiplying. Set the primary's energy and type (proton, iron nucleus, photon) and watch the particle count and the depth of maximum: ten times the energy gives ten times the particles at maximum and pushes the maximum deeper by a fixed step, while an iron nucleus, 56 lighter showers at once, peaks higher in the sky. Compare the model's depth of maximum against the energy spectrum and composition trend in the Pierre Auger open data.
takeaway: One particle with the energy of a thrown tennis ball becomes billions in the air, and the depth at which the shower peaks tells both how energetic it was and how heavy it was.
needs: The Pierre Auger Observatory open data (a public release of ten percent of its events with documentation; licence not confirmed in this round).

title: Colliding galaxies

takeaway: Tides, not impacts, shape colliding galaxies, so a slow pass in the direction of a disc's spin throws its stars into long tails while the same pass against the spin leaves it almost untouched.

title: Inflation & the horizon problem

A second plot shows the curvature parameter driven toward zero by the same phase.
takeaway: A brief period of accelerating expansion lets the whole observable universe come from a patch that was once in causal contact.

title: The three-body problem & Lagrange points
interaction: The circular restricted three-body problem drawn in the frame that rotates with the two large bodies. Set the mass ratio (Sun-Earth, Earth-Moon) and the five Lagrange points appear; set the probe's energy (the Jacobi constant) and the forbidden regions shade in, opening gates at L1 and L2 as the energy rises. Drop a probe at L1 or L2 and it drifts away within months, drop one at L4 and it wanders in a tadpole around the point for as long as the reader waits, as Jupiter's Trojans do, and nudge a starting position by a hair to run two probes side by side and watch their paths split.
takeaway: With three bodies there is no formula for the motion, but there are five points where a small body can sit, three balanced on a knife edge and two stable, and an energy map says where it can and cannot go.
pitfall: L1 and L2 are not places where gravity cancels; a spacecraft there orbits the Sun with Earth's period because the two pulls add to exactly the needed centripetal force, and it still needs station-keeping.

title: Neutron stars & pulsars

title: Stellar spectra & the Saha equation
interaction: Slide a star's surface temperature from 3,000 to 40,000 kelvin. title: Tidal locking & orbital resonance
interaction: A planet and a moon, each raising a tidal bulge on the other that lags by an amount the reader sets through the tidal quality factor. Run the secular equations: the moon's spin slows until it shows one face to the planet, the planet's day lengthens and the moon drifts outward, with the Moon's 3.8 centimeters a year drawn to scale.
